nameStory: This fungus earned the name 'artist's bracket' because its white undersurface can be scratched or drawn on like a natural canvas, turning brown where touched. Artists and nature crafters have used these woody brackets for centuries to create detailed drawings and etchings that last for years. The alternate name 'bear bread' comes from the old belief that bears would gnaw on these tough, cork-like fungi.
description: Artist's bracket is a hard, woody shelf fungus that grows horizontally from tree trunks and fallen logs like a natural shelf or bracket. These perennial fungi can grow quite large, sometimes reaching dinner plate size or bigger, with a distinctive white margin around a brownish top surface. The bracket has a thick, cork-like texture and can persist for many years, adding new layers of growth annually. Unlike mushrooms with gills, the underside has tiny pores instead of gills.

idTips.label: Pores
idTips.description: The white underside is covered in tiny pores (not gills) that bruise brown when scratched or pressed, making it perfect for natural artwork

idTips.label: Cap
idTips.description: Hard, woody bracket with concentric ridges on top, grayish-brown to reddish-brown with a distinctive white growing edge

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Feels like cork or hard wood when touched - you could knock on it like a door and hear a solid thunk

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: No stem - grows directly from wood in shelf-like brackets that can be stacked in tiers

idTips.label: Spore Print
idTips.description: Releases rusty-brown spores that often coat the upper surface, giving it a dusty appearance

idTips.label: Smell
idTips.description: Fresh specimens have a pleasant, earthy mushroom smell, while older ones may smell slightly sour or musty

habitat: Look for artist's bracket on dead or dying hardwood trees throughout New England's forests, parks, and wooded areas. It's especially common on maple, oak, birch, and beech trees, both on standing dead trees and fallen logs. You'll find it from sea level to mountain elevations, often in the same spots year after year since the brackets can persist for decades.

seasonality.spring: Existing brackets continue growing with fresh white edges appearing. New brackets may begin forming on recently dead trees.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season with bright white margins most noticeable. Spore release is heaviest, often coating nearby surfaces with brown dust.
seasonality.fall: Growth slows but brackets remain prominent. This is prime time for nature artists since the pore surface is most responsive to scratching.
seasonality.winter: Brackets persist and remain identifiable under snow. The cork-like texture helps them survive freezing temperatures without damage.

funFact: Artist's bracket can live for over 50 years, adding a new layer of growth each year like tree rings - scientists have used these annual layers to study past climate conditions and forest history.
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with hemlock varnish shelf, which has a shiny, lacquered appearance on top (like it's been painted with varnish) versus artist's bracket's matte, chalky surface. Memory trick: if it looks like someone polished it with furniture wax, it's probably hemlock varnish shelf.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'bracket fungi,' these are completely different from the bracket used in carpentry. The fungal bracket refers to the shelf-like shape. Also, while related to the prized reishi mushrooms used in traditional medicine, artist's bracket is too tough and woody to be edible.
compareHints: Among its Ganoderma relatives in New England, artist's bracket is distinguished by its matte, non-shiny upper surface and prominent white growing edge. Hemlock varnish shelf has that characteristic glossy, varnish-like top surface, while golden reishi has a more yellowish coloration. Artist's bracket also tends to be the largest and most persistent of the group.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among the Ganoderma species in New England, hemlock varnish shelf is distinguished by its glossy, lacquered cap surface and preference for conifers, especially hemlocks.
Unlike its cousin the artist's bracket which stays chalky white and can be drawn on, sessile reishi develops that telltale glossy coating.
Golden reishi differs from artist's bracket by having a much shinier, more colorful surface - artist's bracket is typically gray-brown and chalky rather than glossy.
